name: Buy a Feature
use_case: Customers, residents or members ask for much more than the budget can pay for, and in one-to-one conversations they mark nearly every wish as essential. A game hands each player an equal share of play money and a menu of priced options; some options are dearer than any single player can afford, so players have to club together and persuade each other. What sells, what draws a coalition and what stays on the shelf reveals the trade-offs the group accepts together.
strengths: a real price on each option forces the trade-off that a rating scale lets people avoid
items priced beyond any one budget make participants explain their reasons to each other, and those conversations are the richest result
options that nobody pays for are as informative as the ones that sell out
easy to explain and engaging for customers, residents or members with no planning background
several tables playing the same menu show whether a choice is shared widely or specific to one group
weaknesses: the prices steer the outcome, so a poorly costed menu produces a misleading result
confident negotiators can pull a table towards their own favourites
the menu only contains what the organisers thought of; missing options cannot be bought
the budget size needs care: too much money removes the tension, too little leaves people unable to buy anything they care about
the result shows what one group would fund in one session, not a binding decision or a representative survey
a large menu overwhelms players; it works best with roughly a dozen to thirty options
use_cases: Every time we survey our users about the roadmap, almost every feature comes back rated very important, so the answers tell us nothing about what they would sacrifice when only a handful can be built this year.

Our clients ask for many more improvements than our developers can deliver in a year, and each of them insists that their own request cannot wait. I want them to see what each request costs and to decide with one another which few are worth the money.

Whenever we ask our customers what they need from us next, the answer is all of it; a wish list without prices tells us nothing about which items they would really pay for if their money ran out halfway down the list.

A city wants to hear residents on next year's spending, but a questionnaire lets people tick parks, libraries, road repairs and more police all at once; it wants small tables of residents to hold a fixed sum that cannot cover everything and settle among themselves what to fund.

The student council has a fixed sum for this school year and far more requests than it can pay for; the teacher who supports it wants the students to bargain over the choices with that money in hand instead of voting on each request separately.

A charity's members each back a favourite cause for next year's grants, yet the grant fund covers only a few; the board wants members to spend a share of it in a game and to team up on the costly projects, so the debate turns on what each choice costs the others.

The tenants of our housing cooperative have a long list of wishes for the shared spaces, from a playground to bicycle storage, but the renovation fund pays for only a few of them; the committee wants the tenants to work out among themselves which ones to pay for.
